Originally, Arjovsky et al.  [1] argued that the Wasserstein distance was superior to many others typically used for GANs.  An important feature of WGANs is the requirement for the discriminator to be 1-Lipschitz,  which [1] achieved simply by clipping the network weights.  Recently, Gulrajani et al. [2] proposed a gradient penalty "encouraging" the discriminator to be 1-Lipschitz.  However, their approach estimated continuity on points between the generated and the real samples,  and thus could fail to guarantee Lipschitz-ness at the early training stages.  The paper under review overcomes this drawback by estimating the continuity on perturbations of the real samples.  Together with various technical improvements, this leads to state-of-the-art practical performance both in terms of generated images and in semi-supervised learning.   In terms of novelty, the paper provides one core conceptual idea followed by several tweaks aimed at improving the practical performance of GANs.  The key conceptual idea is to perturb each data point twice and use a Lipschitz constant to bound the difference in the discriminator’s response on the perturbed points.   The proposed method is used in eq. (6) together with the gradient penalty from [2].  The authors found that directly perturbing the data with Gaussian noise led to inferior results  and therefore propose to perturb the hidden layers using dropout.  For supervised learning they demonstrate less overfitting for both MNIST and CIFAR 10.   They also extend their framework to the semi-supervised setting of Salismans et al 2016 and report improved image generation.  The authors do an excellent comparative job in presenting their experiments.  They compare numerous techniques (e.g., Gaussian noise, dropout) and demonstrates the applicability of the approach for a wide range of tasks.  They use several criteria to evaluate their performance (images, inception score, semi-supervised learning, overfitting, weight histogram) and compare against a wide range of competing papers. Almost all progress is incremental,  and the authors modestly give credit to both [1] and [2],  but the title is neither memorable nor useful in expressing the novel idea. Subject: Just Another Day in the Life of Galaxy Whisperers

Hey Team,

So, guess what? The universe decided to throw us a little party, and we RSVP'd with a paper that's basically the Beyoncé of galaxy catalogues. Yeah, you heard it right. We've got a whopping 20 million galaxies strutting their stuff in our latest and greatest morphological classification catalogue. It's like the Met Gala of the cosmos, and we're the ones holding the guest list.

Thanks to the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 data and our trusty sidekick, the Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), we've managed to pull off this little miracle. We've got monochromatic $i$-band DES images doing the cha-cha with linear, logarithmic, and gradient scales. And let's not forget the debiased visual classifications from the Galaxy Zoo 1 catalogue, because who doesn't love a good throwback?

Our CNN models are trained on the crème de la crème of bright galaxies ($16\le{i}<18$) at low redshift ($z<0.25$). But wait, there's more! We're pushing the boundaries of accuracy like a toddler with a new set of crayons, applying our predictions to galaxies at fainter magnitudes and higher redshifts. Our final catalogue is like the Swiss Army knife of galaxy data, covering magnitudes $16\le{i}<21$ and redshifts $z<1.0$. And just to keep things spicy, we're predicting probabilities for two galaxy types: Ellipticals and Spirals. Because why not?

Our CNN classifications are so accurate, they make a Swiss watch look like a sundial. We're talking over 99% accuracy for bright galaxies when compared with the GZ1 classifications ($i<18$). For those fainter galaxies, our visual classification team (a.k.a. three of our co-authors) discovered that our CNN classifier is basically a mind reader. It correctly categorizes those sneaky disky galaxies with rounder and blurred features that humans often mistake for Ellipticals. Who knew AI could be so judgy?

And because we're nothing if not thorough, we've conducted one of the largest examinations of non-parametric methods ever. We're talking about a casual 100,000 galaxies with the same coverage of magnitude and redshift as our training set. Turns out, the Gini coefficient is the best single parameter discriminator between Ellipticals and Spirals for this data set. Who knew a statistician's favorite dessert could be so useful?

So, there you have it. Another day, another galaxy catalogue. No big deal. Just us, casually redefining the universe one CNN model at a time.
